questions.q: Why do we usually prefer a small reward now over a bigger one later?
a: Waiting brings uncertainty, which we dislike
We value small rewards more highly
We forget larger rewards over time
We distrust the people making offers
questions.why: Lesson 1 says an available reward makes bigger delayed rewards less appealing because the wait feels risky.

questions.q: In Thaler's apple study, what did most people choose when the rewards were immediate?
a: One apple today over two tomorrow
Two apples tomorrow over one today
Two apples next year over one today
No apples under either offer
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts distant choices, where people wait for more, with immediate ones, where they grab the single apple.

questions.q: What does the summary say we are willing to risk losing?
a: Things we do not have yet
Things we value most
Things we worked hardest for
Things that belong to others
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains that future gains feel safe to gamble, which is why saving for retirement is so hard.

questions.q: How does the Save More Tomorrow program work?
a: People commit future raises to savings
People deposit a fixed sum each month
Employers match employee contributions
The government adds a bonus at retirement
questions.why: Lesson 2 says participants agree to save a slice of income only if they get a raise, so nothing is taken today.

questions.q: Why do big sticks work better than little carrots?
a: We work harder to avoid losses than to chase gains
Punishments cost less to administer
Rewards are taxed more heavily
People forget rewards very quickly
questions.why: Lesson 3 says we spend more energy avoiding loss, so a heavy penalty changes behavior more than a reward.
